newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian papers welcome frank Yeltsin heart news.
newsitem.headline: Russian papers welcome frank Yeltsin heart news.

text.p: Russian newspapers, near the top of the list of those who have been speculating about the health of Boris Yeltsin, on Friday welcomed the Russian president's frank admission that he needed an operation on his heart.

"The rumours about an imminent operation, which have been circulating since the election campaign, have been confirmed by the president himself," the liberal daily Sevodnya said in a front-page article.
Reminding readers of the break with the secrecy typical in Soviet days, Sevodnya said the disclosure was "a fact unprecedented in our political history".
Yeltsin, 65, said in a television interview on Thursday that he had agreed to have an operation on his heart rather than retreat from the public eye and face a "passive" life.
Calling for a society based on truth, he said the operation would probably take place at the end of September in Moscow.
The announcement broke with Soviet tradition, under which all news about the health of Kremlin leaders was kept under tightly guarded wraps.

When hardline communist leader Leonid Brezhnev was in his decline, the Kremlin falsified pictures and staged events to hide his ill health. In the months before his successor Yuri Andropov died, officials said merely that he had a cold.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta said Yeltsin's news should not have been a surprise at all.
"Yesterday evening came the news that the president will have a heart operation," the paper wrote. "This state secret has hardly been a secret for anyone for a long time.

"Despite this, all the officials stubbornly denied it, even when the question was put to them point blank. They tried to explain away the President's serious illness as nothing more than fatigue after the election campaign," it went on.

Both papers speculated on the political implications which would be raised as Yeltsin recovered from his operation, which could be a relatively simple bypass operation, or could be something more complicated.
The Kremlin has given no details of what precisely is wrong with the president.

"The operation automatically brings up the question -- as called for under the constitution -- of handing the head of state's power temporarily over to Prime Minister Victor Chernomyrdin," Nezavisimaya Gazeta wrote.
"But the question remains whether this will be done officially, as of course should be the case."
Sevodnya said the disclosure showed that Yeltsin trusted the durability of his relationship with both Chernomyrdin and the Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais.
But no power vacuum was likely, the paper added.
Under the constitution, the prime minister takes over when the president is incapacitated.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta, looking back to the election campaign, said the outcome could have been completely different, if voters had known about Yeltsin's health problems before the poll.
Yeltsin finished 14 points ahead of communist Gennady Zyuganov in the runoff ballot on July 3, despite cancelling a string of appearances in the week before the vote.
